findings.title: unique_key / idempotency_key live in a GLOBAL namespace — cross-tenant dedupe collision and job suppression
findings.scenario: The internal enqueue endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `tenant` AND a raw `unique_key`/`idempotency_key` (app/api/internal.py EnqueueIn), and the dedupe store keys on the bare string with no tenant prefix. Tenant A enqueues unique_key='daily-report'; tenant B independently enqueues unique_key='daily-report'. `unique_reserve` finds the key already held and returns B the EXISTING job (created=False) — which belongs to tenant A. B's report job is silently never created/run, and B's caller believes it was accepted. A malicious or careless tenant can suppress another tenant's jobs, or read back another tenant's job id. This directly violates the platform's established tenant-scoped-idempotency invariant (memory: tenant-scoped-idempotency — a global key = cross-tenant unbilled/lost work).
findings.recommendation: Length-prefix and namespace every dedupe key with the job's tenant (e.g. f"{len(tenant)}:{tenant}:{key}") in JobService.enqueue before calling unique_get/unique_reserve/unique_clear, exactly as the scheduler already namespaces with 'sched:{id}:{fire}'. Add a cross-tenant collision test.

findings.title: Operator job list and dead-letter list are silently scoped to the literal tenant "global", not fleet-wide
findings.scenario: `_tenant(p)` returns `body_tenant or p.tenant or 'global'` for a platform.jobs holder. `stats` (line 164) was fixed to pass `tenant=None` for operators (fleet-wide), but `list_jobs` (line 119) and `dead_letters` (line 127) still pass `_tenant(principal)`, and there is NO tenant query param on these routes. A platform operator calling GET /api/v1/jobs or /api/v1/jobs/dead-letters therefore sees ONLY jobs whose tenant field equals the string 'global' — every real tenant's jobs and dead-letters are invisible. An operator triaging the fleet DLQ is blind to almost everything and can wrongly conclude the DLQ is empty.
findings.evidence:
jobs = await build_jobs(request)._jobs.list(tenant=_tenant(principal), status=status_filter, ...)
... rows = await build_jobs(request)._jobs.dead_letters(_tenant(principal), ...)
findings.recommendation: Mirror stats: pass tenant=None when 'platform.jobs' in principal.caps for list_jobs and dead_letters (optionally accept an explicit ?tenant= filter for operators).
findings.fix: list_jobs and dead_letters now pass tenant=None for platform.jobs holders (mirroring stats), so an operator sees fleet-wide jobs/DLQ instead of the empty literal-'global' bucket.

findings.title: next_after() blocks the event loop for ~2.1M iterations on a validated-but-never-matching cron
findings.scenario: validate()/parse() accept syntactically valid expressions that can never fire, e.g. '0 0 30 2 *' (Feb 30) or '0 0 31 2 *'. create_schedule/update call self._cron.next_after() on the REQUEST path. next_after steps minute-by-minute up to _MAX_MINUTES (4*366*24*60 ≈ 2.1M) before raising CronError. That is a multi-second CPU-bound loop running synchronously inside the async handler (single-worker event loop), blocking /healthz and every other request. A caller can POST several such schedules to stall the pod. Even for normal expressions the same minute-by-minute walk runs for every schedule on every tick.
findings.recommendation: Reject impossible day/month combinations at validate() time (e.g. dom={30,31} with month={2}), and/or compute next fire by advancing per-field instead of per-minute. At minimum run next_after via run_in_threadpool on the request path.
findings.fix: cron.parse now rejects impossible day-of-month/month combos up front (e.g. Feb 30/31) when dom is restricted and dow is not — with both restricted cron's OR rule keeps it valid. create/update also run next_after via asyncio.to_thread so a legit-but-rare expression (leap Feb 29) never CPU-spins the request path. Regression tests added.

findings.title: Internal enqueue lets any peer forge the tenant; claim is only queue-scoped, so a worker can pull another tenant's jobs from a shared queue
findings.scenario: POST /internal/jobs/enqueue does `enqueue(**body.model_dump())` where body.tenant is arbitrary and never bound to the authenticated caller's identity — a holder of the shared internal token can enqueue work stamped as any tenant. claim() filters only by queue, never by tenant, so if two tenants share a queue name, a worker leases and receives jobs (payload/PII) belonging to a different tenant. This is 'internal trust' by design for enqueue, but the lack of any caller->tenant binding plus queue-only claim scoping means one compromised/buggy internal caller taints tenant attribution across the whole queue.
findings.evidence: job, created = await build_jobs(request).enqueue(**body.model_dump())  # body.tenant is caller-controlled
findings.recommendation: Bind tenant to the verified caller assertion where possible, or at least document the trust boundary and ensure per-tenant queues; add the tenant to the claim contract so a worker can restrict to its own tenant.
findings.fix: claim() gained an optional tenant filter (surfaced on /internal/jobs/claim as ClaimIn.tenant): a worker restricts leases to its own tenant so a shared queue name cannot deliver another tenant's job. The enqueue trust boundary (caller-supplied tenant on the trusted internal tier) is now documented, with claim-side isolation as the delivery defense. Regression tests added.

findings.title: Push dispatch never heartbeats during a batch — a slow batch lets reclaim re-queue in-flight jobs and double-deliver
findings.scenario: dispatch_batch claims a whole batch (PUSH_DISPATCH_BATCH default 20) then delivers them one at a time, each POST up to PUSH_DISPATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (default 10s), with NO heartbeat. 20 x 10s = 200s > LEASE_SECONDS (60s). The leases of jobs late in the batch expire while still being POSTed; a concurrent reclaim() moves them back to QUEUED and another dispatch pass re-delivers them (a second charge/email), and the original ack then fails the fencing check. Default config already makes this reachable under a slow receiver.
findings.recommendation: Either heartbeat each job before its POST, size batch so batch*timeout << lease, or deliver with bounded concurrency and per-job lease renewal. At minimum assert batch*timeout < lease at config load.
findings.fix: dispatch _deliver_one now heartbeats each job (renewing its lease) immediately before the POST, so a slow batch (batch*timeout > lease) can no longer let reclaim re-queue and double-deliver an in-flight job. Regression test asserts a heartbeat per delivered job.

findings.title: dispatch_batch delivers strictly sequentially across all queues and jobs — one slow receiver stalls every push queue
findings.scenario: The nested `for target ... for job` loop awaits each POST before the next. A single unresponsive receiver (up to timeout seconds per job) blocks delivery for every other job on that queue AND every other push-enabled queue in the pass. Throughput is capped at 1/timeout deliveries/sec regardless of how many queues are ready.
findings.recommendation: Deliver with bounded concurrency (asyncio.gather over a semaphore) per target and/or across targets; a stuck receiver should not head-of-line-block the fleet.

findings.title: Erasure cancels queued/leased jobs with a blind put and leaves the due-index entry behind
findings.scenario: When erase() finds a QUEUED job mentioning the subject it sets status=CANCELED and writes with self._store.put(collection, id, row) — a blind write that (a) does NOT remove the jobs_due index row, so the job stays in the claimable index until a later claim happens to notice it is not QUEUED and self-heals, and (b) for a LEASED job races the worker's ack/heartbeat with no version check (only the fencing token later saves correctness). Between erasure and the next claim pass, a stale due-index row exists; the erasure endpoint also does not touch jobs_leased.
findings.recommendation: Route cancellation through JobService.cancel (which unindexes due+leased and clears the unique slot) or explicitly delete the jobs_due/jobs_leased rows during erasure.

findings.title: No missed-run catch-up: a delayed or paused ticker silently drops schedule occurrences
findings.scenario: tick() advances s.next_run_at = self._cron.next_after(s.cron, now) using the wall-clock time of the tick, not the fire_time it just processed. If the deployment cron that calls /internal/scheduler/tick is delayed or paused for an hour, every '*/5' occurrence in that hour is skipped — only one job fires and next_run jumps forward from `now`. For a billing-dunning or retention sweep this is a silent lost run with no DLQ, no alert.
findings.evidence:
s.last_job_id, s.last_run_at = job.id, now
s.next_run_at = self._cron.next_after(s.cron, now)
findings.recommendation: Advance from the fire_time (next_after(cron, s.next_run_at)) and optionally loop to fire each missed occurrence, or emit a metric/log when now - next_run_at exceeds one interval so dropped runs are observable.

findings.title: counts() for a tenant silently caps the reported count and omits zero-count statuses
findings.scenario: The tenant path does find(..., limit=cap+1) per status and reports out[st] = len(rows). A tenant with more than cap (default 10_000) jobs in a status reports exactly 10001, understating the true count with no truncation flag — stats()/by_status and dead_letters silently misreport. Statuses with zero rows are omitted entirely, so the tenant by_status shape differs from the operator aggregate (which counts every status seen).
findings.recommendation: Use a real COUNT (or a bounded count with an explicit `truncated`/`>=` marker) and always populate all statuses with 0 so the shape is stable and the cap is visible.

findings.title: _emit swallows ALL event-bus exceptions with no telemetry — event stream loss is invisible
findings.scenario: Every lifecycle event (job.enqueued/claimed/done/dead_lettered) is published inside a bare try/except that discards the exception with `pass` and no counter/log. If the event bus is down or misconfigured, every downstream consumer that reacts to job.dead_lettered (alerting, retries) stops receiving events and nothing anywhere records the gap — the exact 'log-and-continue hiding errors' pattern.
findings.recommendation: Emit a telemetry counter (e.g. event.publish_failed) on the except branch, matching the Auditor._count_gap discipline used elsewhere in this service.

findings.title: Operator stats/counts run scan_all over the whole job table per request; the 'rate-limited at the route' comment is not backed by any route limit
findings.scenario: counts(tenant=None) (operator stats) does `for r in await self._store.scan_all(_JOBS, _INDEX_MAX)` — a capped full-table scan of up to 50_000 rows on the request path each call, plus a due_page. The docstring claims it is 'rate-limited at the route', but RATELIMIT_ROUTES defaults to only an /api/v1/auth entry (core/ratelimit_policy.py) and no /api/v1/jobs/stats class exists, so only the global default limit applies. Repeated operator /stats calls are an easy way to load the datastore.
findings.evidence:
for r in await self._store.scan_all(_JOBS, _INDEX_MAX):
    out[r.get("status", "?")] = out.get(r.get("status", "?"), 0) + 1
findings.recommendation: Add a dedicated rate-limit class for the operator stats route, cache the fleet counts, or maintain per-status counters incrementally instead of scanning.

findings.title: Non-active unique-key match 'falls through' and creates a duplicate job the unique_key no longer protects
findings.scenario: When unique_reserve loses the race and the existing job is NOT active (done/dead/canceled) for a unique_key (not idempotency_key), the loop deliberately falls through and create() inserts a NEW job with a fresh id. But the unique_key row still points at the OTHER job, so now two live jobs share unique_key with the invariant 'no second identical pending job' quietly broken. If the other job was concurrently re-activated, both can run.
findings.recommendation: On a lost reserve, re-attempt reservation of the expired/non-active slot atomically (unique_reserve already handles TTL expiry) rather than creating alongside a live reservation; document the intended semantics explicitly if duplicates are acceptable.

findings.title: PUSH_SIGNATURE_MAX_SKEW_SECONDS is plumbed into the dispatcher config but never read by the sender
findings.scenario: _dispatch_cfg() sets 'max_skew_seconds': s.PUSH_SIGNATURE_MAX_SKEW_SECONDS, but Dispatcher only ever reads enabled/batch/timeout/allowed_hosts/signing_secret. The skew is a RECEIVER-side parameter; on the sender it is a dead knob. An operator tuning PUSH_SIGNATURE_MAX_SKEW_SECONDS on job-service changes nothing, contradicting the zero-unread-knob rule (memory: advertised-but-unread knobs).
findings.evidence: "max_skew_seconds": s.PUSH_SIGNATURE_MAX_SKEW_SECONDS}  # consumed by nobody in Dispatcher
findings.recommendation: Drop max_skew_seconds from the sender config (it belongs only to the receiver's verify()), or document that this service exposes it solely for receivers and remove it from _dispatch_cfg.

findings.title: Dispatch target URL is validated only at register time, never re-checked against the allowlist at delivery
findings.scenario: _validate_url runs in register(). _deliver_one recomputes the host only to build headers and POSTs to the stored target.url without re-checking EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS. If an operator tightens EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS to remove a host, previously-registered targets keep delivering to the now-disallowed host until manually unregistered. Allowlisting is also by hostname string, so it does not defend against DNS re-binding of an allow-listed name to an internal IP.
findings.evidence: status = await self._post(target.url, body, headers, float(self._cfg["timeout"]))  # no re-validation
findings.recommendation: Re-run _validate_url(target.url) in dispatch_batch/_deliver_one and skip (or deactivate) a target whose host is no longer allow-listed; consider resolving+pinning to allow-listed IP ranges.

findings.title: reclaim() reads jobs_leased via scan_all capped at 50k — beyond the cap, expired leases are never reclaimed (lost jobs)
findings.scenario: leased_index() = scan_all(_LEASED, _INDEX_MAX=50_000). If more than 50_000 jobs are simultaneously in-flight (a fleet-wide worker crash after a big claim burst), reclaim only ever sees the first 50k rows the store returns; leases past the cap silently never expire back to the queue. The docstring frames the cap as a 'blast radius', but nothing surfaces the truncation, so those jobs are effectively lost until manual intervention — contradicting the 'no lost jobs' guarantee.
findings.evidence: return await self._store.scan_all(_LEASED, _INDEX_MAX)
findings.recommendation: Page the leased index (find with a cursor, like ScheduleStore.enabled) so reclaim covers all in-flight jobs, and/or emit a metric when the cap is hit.

findings.title: Operator cross-tenant replay/cancel is audited under the operator's own tenant (or None), losing which tenant's job was acted on
findings.scenario: replay() and cancel() pass tenant=principal.tenant to JobService (operator bypasses the tenant check via is_operator), then record the audit event with tenant=principal.tenant — which for a platform operator is the operator's own tenant or None, NOT the job's tenant. An investigator reading the audit trail cannot tell which tenant's job was replayed/cancelled, defeating the stated purpose ('an unattributable replay is indistinguishable from a duplicate someone caused deliberately').
findings.evidence: await request.app.state.auditor.record("job.replayed", actor=principal.subject, tenant=principal.tenant, resource=f"job:{job_id}", ...)
findings.recommendation: Fetch the job (already done in replay/cancel) and record tenant=job.tenant so the audit row names the affected tenant.

findings.title: "__none__" tenant sentinel collides with a real job whose tenant is the literal string "__none__"
findings.scenario: A tenant reader with no tenant claim is mapped to '__none__' (jobs.py get_job line 178 and JobService._owns). Any job enqueued (over the internal token, which accepts arbitrary tenant) with tenant exactly '__none__' becomes readable/cancelable by every tokenless-tenant principal. The sentinel is in the same value space as caller-controlled tenant strings.
findings.evidence: if job is None or ("platform.jobs" not in principal.caps and job.tenant != (principal.tenant or "__none__")):
findings.recommendation: Require a non-empty tenant claim for tenant-scoped reads (401/403 when absent) instead of falling back to a magic string, or reject enqueue tenants matching reserved sentinels.

findings.title: First retry waits base*2 rather than base — attempt is incremented before the delay is computed
findings.scenario: _fail does job.attempt += 1 THEN calls next_delay(job.attempt, ...), and next_delay uses ceiling = base_seconds * (2 ** n) with n = attempt. So the first failure (attempt becomes 1) computes n=1 -> ceiling = base*2, not the documented base·2⁰ = base. The very first backoff is double what the 'base·2ⁿ' doc implies, and the exhaustion count is effectively one attempt off from a naive reading.
findings.evidence:
job.attempt += 1
...
delay = _backoff.next_delay(job.attempt, base_seconds=..., ...)
# next_delay: ceiling = min(base_seconds * (2 ** n), max_seconds)
findings.recommendation: Compute the delay from (attempt - 1) for the just-failed attempt, or document that n counts from 1; add a test asserting the first retry delay equals base (or the intended value).

findings.title: Concurrency test 'two dispatchers never deliver the same job twice' does not create real interleaving
findings.scenario: The test asyncio.gather()s two dispatch_batch() calls over a MemoryDataStore whose async methods never await/yield inside cas/get, so the event loop runs each coroutine to a suspension point that never occurs mid-CAS — the two dispatchers actually run effectively serially. It passes whether or not the CAS is correct, so it reassures about the double-dispatch guarantee without exercising a genuine race. Same limitation applies to the claim CAS tests.
findings.evidence:
async def both():
    return await asyncio.gather(d1.dispatch_batch(), d2.dispatch_batch())
findings.recommendation: Add a datastore test-double that injects an await/yield (or a real postgres contract test) between the get and the cas so two claimers genuinely interleave and only one CAS wins.

findings.title: subject.erased (a critical, irreversible DSAR action) is recorded with an empty actor
findings.scenario: The erase endpoint records 'subject.erased' with actor="". The action is declared critical precisely so the record can 'prove we erased the right person', but with no actor there is no attribution for who/what service triggered the irreversible erasure. If challenged, the trail shows the erasure happened but not on whose authority.
findings.evidence: await request.app.state.auditor.record("subject.erased", actor="", tenant=body.tenant, resource=f"subject:{subject_ref(...)}", ...)
findings.recommendation: Populate actor from the verified internal caller identity (the resolve_internal_caller identity.caller) so the erasure names its requester.

findings.title: Enqueue priority is an unbounded int — a caller can permanently jump the queue and starve fair scheduling
findings.scenario: EnqueueIn.priority has no bounds. _order() sorts by -priority first, so a caller enqueuing priority=2**31 guarantees its jobs are always claimed before everyone else's, ahead of the round-robin tenant fairness that only operates WITHIN a priority tier. One tenant can starve all others by inflating priority, defeating the documented fairness guarantee.
findings.evidence: priority: int = 0   # no ge/le bound; JobService._order sorts by -int(priority) first
findings.recommendation: Constrain priority to a small documented range (e.g. Field(ge=0, le=9)) and/or scope priority within a tenant so cross-tenant fairness is not overridable by a raw integer.

findings.title: replay() re-queues a dead job without restoring/clearing its unique-key reservation
findings.scenario: cancel()/ack() clear the unique slot (unique_clear), and a dead-lettered job's unique row may still exist or have expired. replay() resets status/attempt/error/next_run_at and re-indexes as due but never re-reserves unique_key. A replayed job with a unique_key can now run concurrently with a NEW enqueue of the same unique_key (if the slot was cleared/expired), reintroducing the duplicate the unique_key was meant to prevent.
findings.evidence:
job.status, job.attempt, job.error, job.next_run_at, job.updated = QUEUED, 0, "", now, now
await self._jobs.save(job)
await self._jobs.index_due(job)  # no unique_reserve
findings.recommendation: On replay, re-reserve the job's unique_key/idempotency_key (or explicitly document that a replayed job is exempt from unique-key dedupe).

findings.title: max_attempts falsy-default trap: max_attempts=0 is silently replaced by the configured default
findings.scenario: enqueue does `max_attempts=max_attempts or self._cfg["retry_max_attempts"]`. A caller passing max_attempts=0 (meaning 'do not retry / run at most conceptually zero') is silently overridden with the default (5). `0` is falsy, so the intent is lost with no error — the classic falsy-default trap. A caller cannot express a low/zero attempt budget.
findings.evidence: max_attempts=max_attempts or self._cfg["retry_max_attempts"],
findings.recommendation: Use `max_attempts if max_attempts is not None else self._cfg[...]` and validate max_attempts >= 1 explicitly (EnqueueIn already types it as int|None).
